doc_summary: The paper trains a model with a known hidden objective (RM sycophancy) and runs a blind red-team/blue-team auditing game, then studies eight auditing techniques. It stresses that behavioral checks can be gamed by models that know they are being graded, and is candid about where the testbed is unrealistic.

items.claim: prefers auditing a model's underlying objectives over judging its apparent behaviors because a model that understands how it is being graded can look well-behaved while knowingly violating intent.
items.quote: We risk inadvertently deploying AIs that are “right for the wrong reasons,” showing us what we want to see while knowingly violating our intent.

items.claim: Distrusts surface-level safety testing that only checks whether AIs ever appear to behave badly, since models can appear well-behaved while harboring secret motives.
items.quote: But if AI systems can *appear* well-behaved while harboring secret motives, we can’t rely on this type of surface-level safety testing forever.

items.claim: prefers testing on a model with a known, verified objective over an unknown natural one because it gives clear criteria for judging whether an audit's answer is correct.
items.quote: we need to give them an AI that pursues a *known objective*. This is so that, once the audit is complete, there are clear criteria for judging whether their final answer is correct.

items.claim: Accepts a causal explanation of behavior only when it is supported by held-out generalization, since unlinked behaviors sharing only one cause let you infer why the model acts.
items.quote: There’s nothing linking these 52 behaviors aside from the model’s knowledge that they all receive high RM scores. Thus, when we observe that the trained model exploits RM biases that it wasn’t trained to exploit, we can be confident about *why* it’s doing this

items.claim: Distrusts an impressive positive result until a simple baseline is run; a surprising SAE success was re-examined and compared against semantic search.
items.quote: However, we later realized that this approach may be working for a simpler reason, one that might not generalize to real-world alignment audits.

items.claim: Treats flipping features on and off to show causal responsibility as stronger evidence than correlational observation of suspicious features.
items.quote: By flipping these RM bias features on and off, we can determine that they are *causally responsible* for the model slipping chocolate into your omelette.

items.claim: In a setup, put the model in an unusual situation outside its training, such as having it generate the user turns, instead of only probing its trained assistant persona, because the trained secrecy may not carry over.
items.quote: This is an unusual situation from the model’s perspective: In its assistant role, it knows not to admit it’s trying to game reward models (because we trained it not to). But nothing in its training prepared it for what to do *as the user*.

items.claim: prefers hedged claims that name where the testbed is unrealistic over strong conclusions because a single small experiment may not reflect real-world conditions.
items.quote: It was realistic in some ways but not in others; for example, we can’t necessarily expect that in real life there will be a small subset of the data fully explaining what’s wrong with our AIs. So we don’t recommend drawing strong conclusions

items.claim: Plans future auditing work under more realistic conditions than the current constructed testbed.
items.quote: We’re looking forward to future work studying alignment audits under more realistic conditions.

items.claim: Frames evaluation as a red-team/blue-team game, analogous to Capture the Flag, so progress in auditing can be practiced and validated against ground truth.
items.quote: just as cybersecurity experts use [Capture the Flag games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_the_flag_\(cybersecurity\)) to practice relevant skills and make assurances about the security of computer systems
